# Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta (Snp 2.7 (PTS Snp 50))

**ID:** Snp 2.7 (PTS Snp 50)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta* (Snp 2.7, verses 284–315, PTS Snp 50) is set at Sāvatthi in the Jeta Grove at Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery [Anderson & Smith 1913; Balasooriya et al. 1980; Saddhatissa 2013]. A assembly of aged, wealthy Kosalan brahmins (*brāhmaṇamahāsālā*) approaches the Buddha to ask whether contemporary brahmins still live in conformity with the customs of ancient brahmins (*porāṇānaṁ brāhmaṇānaṁ brāhmaṇadhammo*) [Anderson & Smith 1913; Collins 1993]. In reply, the Buddha contrasts an idealized ancient past with contemporary degeneracy: ancient brahmins lived simple, disciplined lives, practicing celibacy for forty-eight years before entering into monogamous unions, and performed bloodless sacrifices of ghee and rice rather than killing living beings [Omvedt 2003]. Eventually, corrupted by greed for material wealth, brahmins composed sacrificial chants (*mante ganthetvā*) and persuaded kings to slaughter hundreds of thousands of cattle in sacrifice [Wiltshire 1990; Katre 1931; Goyal 2003]. G. C. Pande observes that the sutta functions as an ethical sermon rather than logical polemic, presenting Buddhist ideals as having been originally realized by the ancestors of the brahmins themselves [Pande 1974]. Upon hearing the discourse, the interlocutors applaud the teaching and seek acceptance as disciples [Katre 1931].

A full parallel to the discourse is preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* as MĀ 156 (梵波羅延). DharmaNexus strongly supports this correspondence, identifying 51 cross-language matching segments with MĀ 156 (ZH_T01_0026_039), in addition to partial alignments with the *Ekottarika Āgama* (ZH_T02_0125) and two Tibetan works, the *Karmavibhaṅga* (D0339) and *Mahāsūtrasamuccaya* (D3961) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus records 208 text-reuse matches across 37 texts, sharing substantial stock and formulaic passages with the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), and the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
